```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

In finite mixture modelling, the number of latent classes is not known a
priori and is not a parameter of the model; it must be determined by
comparing models fitted with different numbers of classes. No single
statistic identifies the correct number: information criteria,
likelihood-based tests and indices of classification quality each have known
limitations, and they frequently disagree (Nylund, Asparouhov and Muthén,
2007). Class enumeration is therefore an inferential judgement that
integrates several sources of evidence and is reported transparently. This
guide describes each source of evidence that latents computes for a set of
candidate models: its definition, its interpretation, and the conditions
under which it is unreliable. It then outlines how these sources are combined
into a defensible and reproducible decision. A complete applied example is
given in [Class enumeration in mixture models](class-enumeration.html).

The evidence considered here addresses five distinct questions, summarized
below together with the functions that report it.

| Question | Evidence | Functions |
|---|---|---|
| Which candidate balances fit and size best? | Information criteria and their minima | `as.data.frame()`, `get_results(x, "best")`, `plot_enumeration(x)` |
| Where do added classes stop paying off? | Changes between neighbouring candidates and the knee of each curve | `get_results(x, "deltas")`, `get_results(x, "knees")`, `plot_selection(x, what = "deltas")`, `plot_selection(x, what = "heatmap")` |
| Are the classes distinct? | Entropy, average posterior probability, odds of correct classification | `get_results(x, "classification")`, `plot_selection(x, what = "diagnostics")` |
| Can the estimate be trusted? | Convergence, boundary estimates, replication of the best likelihood, the smallest class | `plot_selection(x, what = "trust")`, `plot_selection(x, what = "smallest")` |
| Is one more class supported? | The bootstrap likelihood ratio test of neighbouring candidates | `bootstrap_lrt()` |

`plot_selection(x)` displays the evidence of the second, third and
fourth rows jointly, and `compare_models()` tabulates selected candidates side
by side.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
```

## The candidates

The examples use `course_engagement`, in which course enrolments are nested
within students and each enrolment is described by five standardized
indicators of activity. A model is fitted for every combination of one to six
profiles and one to four group classes, with class-specific variances and no
covariances (`"VVI"`). Three random starts per candidate are used to limit
computation; applied analyses should use at least ten, because replication of
the maximum likelihood across starts is itself part of the evidence.

```{r enumerate}
activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
models
```

```{r grid-values, include = FALSE}
candidates <- as.data.frame(models)
n_candidates <- nrow(candidates)
n_fitted <- with(candidates, sum(!is.na(log_likelihood)))
n_students <- with(course_engagement, length(unique(student)))
n_enrolments <- nrow(course_engagement)
```

The grid comprises `r n_candidates` candidates, of which `r n_fitted` were
estimated. A model with one profile and several group classes is not
identified, because group classes defined over a single profile cannot
differ; such candidates are listed but not estimated. Each candidate is
labelled by its numbers of classes (e.g., `profiles4_groups3` for four
profiles and three group classes), and the functions below accept this label.

## Before fitting: starts, scaling and missing values

Three analytic decisions precede estimation. Each is passed through the `...`
argument of `enumerate_classes()`, `enumerate_lpa()` and `enumerate_lca()`,
so that it applies identically to every candidate, and each should be
reported alongside the selected number of classes.

### Random starts

The likelihood of a finite mixture model is typically multimodal, and the EM
algorithm converges to a local maximum determined by its starting values.
`n_starts` sets the number of random starts per candidate; increasing it
reduces the probability that a candidate is reported at a local rather than
the global maximum. A solution at a local maximum usually separates its
classes less well, so re-estimation with more starts frequently increases
entropy and AvePP. When more starts are required, the entire grid is
re-estimated with the same number; re-estimating only the candidates of
interest would confer on them an advantage in likelihood and separation that
the remaining candidates were not given.

```{r starts, eval = FALSE}
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 20, seed = 1)
```

Additional starts also make a degenerate solution more likely to be found
when a candidate has more profiles than the data support: one profile
collapses on a single observation, with every variance at its lower bound
(`min_variance`). The Gaussian likelihood of such a profile increases without
limit as its variances shrink, so its value, and every criterion computed
from it, is determined by `min_variance` rather than by the data, and BIC can
favour one profile too many as a result. In a simulation with 500 starts per
candidate, this occurred in two of 29 datasets; with ten or twenty starts it
was rare. Such candidates carry `boundary = TRUE` in the table of
candidates. `boundary = "exclude"` sets aside every start with a variance at
its lower bound and retains the best of the remaining starts; the default,
`"allow"`, retains the highest likelihood, as Mplus does. The option is
advisable when many starts are used, and it has no effect on categorical
indicators, which have no variances. A spurious profile need not reach the
bound: a few nearly coincident observations can give it variances close to
zero. A candidate with a profile that has fewer effective members than its
own means and variances is therefore reported by a `latents_thin_profiles`
warning, which the grid above raises once.

```{r starts-exclude, eval = FALSE}
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 200,
                            boundary = "exclude", seed = 1)
```

### Centring and scaling

`centering` subtracts a mean and `scaling` divides by a standard deviation,
each computed at one of two levels: over all observations (`"grand"`) or
within each group (`"person"`). Combined, they yield the conventional
z-scores. Grand-mean standardization (`centering = "grand", scaling =
"grand"`) expresses each indicator in sample standard deviations;
within-person standardization (`centering = "person", scaling = "person"`)
expresses each observation as a deviation from its own group's mean in units
of that group's standard deviation, so that the profiles describe
within-person fluctuation rather than between-person level.

Under covariance structures that estimate a separate variance for each
indicator (`EEI`, `VVI`, `EEE`, `VVV`, `EVI`, `VEI`), grand-mean scaling is a
reparameterization of the unconstrained likelihood. Corresponding optima have
the same class membership, entropy and AvePP when bounds and priors transform
consistently. The package's absolute variance floor is expressed in the fitted
units, so an active floor can change classification after rescaling; numerical
search can also reach different local optima. The spherical structures `EII` and
`VII` constrain all indicators to a common variance, so that an unscaled
indicator with a large range would dominate the classification; under these
structures the indicators should be standardized beforehand.

```{r scaling}
srl_indicators <- c("cognitive_strategies", "intrinsic_value",
                    "self_efficacy", "self_regulation", "test_anxiety")
spherical <- enumerate_lpa(srl, srl_indicators, n_profiles = 2:4,
                           model = "EII", centering = "grand",
                           scaling = "grand", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
get_results(spherical, "best")
```

Because scaling shifts the log likelihood by a constant, information criteria
are comparable only among candidates estimated under the same centring and
scaling, as is the case within a single grid.

### Missing values

With `missing = "fiml"`, the likelihood of each observation is evaluated over
its observed indicators, without imputation; under the missing-at-random
assumption and a correctly specified, identifiable model, this supports
consistent estimation; it does not guarantee finite-sample unbiasedness.
An observation with all indicators
missing contributes nothing to the likelihood, and its posterior probability
equals the prior implied by its group; it is therefore not classified.
Following Mplus, such observations are excluded from the sample size of the
individual-level information criteria, from entropy and AvePP, from the
classification tables and from the effective class counts; `n_informative`
records the number retained, and the printed fit reports the number
excluded. Groups in which no observation has an observed indicator are
excluded from the group-level sample size and statistics on the same grounds
(`n_informative_groups`), whereas a group with at least one observed row is
retained. Partially observed rows remain in every statistic: they are
classified, with correspondingly greater uncertainty, from the indicators
available. Setting `drop_empty = FALSE` restores the counting rules of latents
0.9.37 and earlier, so that previously reported results can be reproduced.

```{r missing}
set.seed(3)
incomplete <- course_engagement
empty <- sample(nrow(incomplete), 150)
incomplete[empty, activity] <- NA
partial <- setdiff(sample(nrow(incomplete), 150), empty)
incomplete[partial, "attendance"] <- NA
incomplete_fit <- multilpa(incomplete, activity, "student", n_profiles = 3,
                           n_group_classes = 2, model = "VVI",
                           missing = "fiml", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
get_results(incomplete_fit, "entropy")
```

```{r missing-values, include = FALSE}
incomplete_entropy <- get_results(incomplete_fit, "entropy")
classified_rows <- with(subset(incomplete_entropy, level == "individuals"),
                        n_units)
stopifnot(classified_rows == nrow(incomplete) - length(empty))
```

Individual-level entropy is computed over `r classified_rows` observations:
the `r format(nrow(incomplete), big.mark = ",")` enrolments less the
`r length(empty)` with no observed indicator. Deleting those rows from the
data yields identical estimates, likelihood and classification statistics.
Deleting partially observed rows, by contrast, alters the sample and, where
missingness depends on observed values, biases the estimated profiles.

## Information criteria

### Definitions

Each criterion adds a penalty to the deviance, `-2L`, where `L` is the
maximized log likelihood. Let `q` denote the number of free parameters, `n`
the sample size, and `EN = -sum(p log p)` the classification entropy, summed
over all units and classes of the posterior probabilities `p`:

| Criterion | Formula | Penalty depends on | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| `aic` | `-2L + 2q` | parameters only | Akaike (1974) |
| `kic` | `-2L + 3(q + 1)` | parameters only | Cavanaugh (1999), in the form tidyLPA computes; his general `-2L + 3q` differs by a constant 3 |
| `bic` | `-2L + q log(n)` | sample size | Schwarz (1978) |
| `sabic` | `-2L + q log((n + 2) / 24)` | sample size | Sclove (1987) |
| `caic` | `-2L + q (log(n) + 1)` | sample size | Bozdogan (1987) |
| `icl` | `-2L + q log(n) + 2 EN` | sample size and classification | Biernacki, Celeux and Govaert (2000) |
| `awe` | `-2(L - EN) + 2q (1.5 + log(n))` | sample size and classification | Banfield and Raftery (1993) |
| `clc` | `-2L + 2 EN` | classification only | Biernacki and Govaert (1997) |

Smaller values indicate a better trade-off between fit and complexity. The
penalty per parameter is 2 for AIC, 3 for KIC, `log((n + 2) / 24)` for
SABIC, `log(n)` for BIC and `log(n) + 1` for CAIC. SABIC has a smaller
per-parameter penalty than AIC until `n` exceeds `24 * exp(2) - 2`
(approximately 175.34); compare the actual penalties at the relevant sample
size. Heavier penalties favour fewer classes. ICL and AWE additionally penalize
classification uncertainty, since overlapping classes increase `EN`; they
consequently favour fewer and better-separated classes than BIC. CLC carries
no per-parameter penalty, only the entropy term, and may favour many classes
when these are well separated and few when they are not. CLC is defined here,
as are ICL and AWE, on the entropy sum; some software reports a variant based
on relative entropy, which is bounded by one and therefore imposes almost no
penalty, and the two are not comparable.

### Two conventions for the sample size

In a two-level model the sample size may be defined as the number of groups
(here, `r n_students` students) or the number of observations (here,
`r format(n_enrolments, big.mark = ",")` enrolments). latents reports every
sample-size-dependent criterion under both conventions: columns ending in
`_groups` use the number of groups and columns ending in `_individual` the
number of observations. Neither constitutes a uniquely correct multilevel
BIC; each is a stated convention, and an analysis adopts one and applies it to
every candidate. AIC and KIC do not depend on the sample size.

The entropy `EN` of ICL, AWE and CLC is the same under both conventions: the
soft entropy of the complete-data classification, which in a two-level model
is the group class of every student together with the profile of every
enrolment. It is the entropy of the group-class posteriors plus, within each
group class, the entropy of the profile posteriors (Biernacki, Celeux and
Govaert 2000). With one group class it is the entropy of the profile
posteriors. The two conventions therefore differ only in `n`, and in a
single-level model, where the two sample sizes coincide, every criterion is
identical under both. A transition model from `lta()` is the exception: its
profiles form a Markov chain within a person, and its criteria charge one
level's entropy per convention.

### The table of every candidate

`as.data.frame()` returns one row per candidate, containing every criterion
under both conventions together with the log likelihood, the number of
parameters, summaries of classification quality and diagnostics of
estimation.

```{r candidates}
as.data.frame(models)
```

### The minimum of each criterion

`get_results(x, "best")` reduces this table to one row per criterion and
convention, giving the candidate at which the criterion attains its minimum,
its numbers of classes and the minimum value. It identifies the candidate
favoured by each criterion and makes no further inference.

```{r best}
get_results(models, "best")
```

```{r best-values, include = FALSE}
best <- get_results(models, "best")
pick <- function(name, convention_name) {
  with(subset(best, criterion == name & convention %in% convention_name),
       candidate)
}
bic_groups_pick <- pick("bic", "groups")
bic_individual_pick <- pick("bic", "individuals")
icl_groups_pick <- pick("icl", "groups")
aic_pick <- with(subset(best, criterion == "aic"), candidate)
n_distinct_picks <- length(unique(best$candidate))
largest <- with(subset(candidates, !is.na(log_likelihood)),
                sprintf("profiles%d_groups%d", max(n_profiles),
                        max(n_group_classes)))
```

In this example the criteria favour `r n_distinct_picks` different
candidates: BIC with students as units favours `r bic_groups_pick`, BIC with
enrolments as units `r bic_individual_pick`, ICL with students as units
`r icl_groups_pick`, and AIC `r aic_pick`. Such disagreement is typical rather
than anomalous. The criteria were derived for different purposes, and their
penalties largely account for the pattern: AIC, with the lightest penalty,
favours the largest candidate, whereas the entropy-based criteria favour
smaller ones.

A minimum at the boundary of the grid, that is, at the largest number of
profiles or group classes estimated, indicates that the criterion was still
decreasing and that the range examined was too narrow. The range is then
extended until the minimum lies in its interior. Where the criterion
continues to decrease at every size the data can support, as is common in
large samples, the magnitude of successive decreases becomes the relevant
evidence (see below).

### Plotting the criteria

`plot_enumeration()` displays the criteria against the number of profiles, with one line
per number of group classes and the minimum of each criterion marked. `what`
selects criteria by column name, and `what = "all"` displays all of them.

```{r plot-criteria, fig.height = 5}
plot_enumeration(models)
```

```{r plot-bic}
plot_enumeration(models, what = "bic_groups")
```

## Where added classes stop paying off

### Deltas

When a criterion decreases across the entire range, its minimum is
uninformative, but the magnitude of each decrease is not.
`get_results(x, "deltas")` reports, for every candidate, the decrease in a
criterion relative to the neighbouring candidate with one profile fewer
(`delta_profile`, from `from_profile`) and with one group class fewer
(`delta_group_class`, from `from_group_class`). A positive value indicates
that the additional class reduced the criterion, and a negative value that it
increased it; candidates without such a neighbour in the grid have `NA`. BIC
with groups as units is used unless `using` specifies another criterion.

```{r deltas}
get_results(models, "deltas")
```

```{r deltas-values, include = FALSE}
deltas <- get_results(models, "deltas")
delta_of <- function(name) with(subset(deltas, candidate == name),
                                round(delta_profile))
step_3 <- delta_of("profiles3_groups3")
step_4 <- delta_of("profiles4_groups3")
step_5 <- delta_of("profiles5_groups3")
stopifnot(step_3 > step_4, step_4 > 0, step_5 < 0)
```

With three group classes, the third profile reduces BIC by
`r format(step_3, big.mark = ",")` and the fourth by
`r format(step_4, big.mark = ",")`, whereas the fifth increases it by
`r format(-step_5, big.mark = ",")` (shown as a negative decrease). The
candidate with two profiles has no profile-wise delta because its neighbour,
with one profile and three group classes, is not identified. Diminishing
decreases indicate the point beyond which additional profiles capture detail
rather than structure, and the first negative value marks where they cease to
improve the criterion. The deltas are displayed for both directions: along
the number of profiles (left) and along the number of group classes (right).

```{r plot-deltas, fig.height = 5}
plot_selection(models, what = "deltas")
```

The same display is available for any criterion:

```{r plot-deltas-icl, fig.height = 5}
plot_selection(models, what = "deltas", using = "icl_individual")
```

### Knees

The knee, or elbow, of a decreasing curve is the point at which it changes
from steep to flat. `get_results(x, "knees")` locates it with a simplified,
geometric version of the Kneedle algorithm (Satopää, Albrecht, Irwin and
Raghavan, 2011):

1. both axes, the number of classes and the criterion, are rescaled to the
   unit interval;
2. a chord is drawn from the first candidate to the last;
3. the knee is the candidate with the greatest perpendicular distance below
   the chord, and `distance` is that distance in rescaled units.

The smoothing and sensitivity thresholds of the original algorithm are
omitted, so a nearly linear curve may still yield a knee with a very small
`distance`; the distance therefore quantifies the strength of the bend as well
as its location. A curve whose final value is not below its initial value has
no knee, since a bend in an increasing criterion does not indicate
diminishing returns.

Knees are computed along three families of curves: over the number of
profiles at each number of group classes (`direction = "profiles"`), over the
number of group classes at each number of profiles (`"group_classes"`), and
over all candidates ordered by number of parameters (`"parameters"`). The
columns `from` and `to` identify the endpoints of each curve and `n_points`
its length.

```{r knees}
get_results(models, "knees")
```

Because the chord terminates at the largest candidate estimated, the location
of the knee depends on the extent of the grid: adding a candidate moves the
chord and may move the knee. This dependence is assessed directly.
`knee_without_largest` is the knee of the same curve with its final
candidate removed, and `stable` is `TRUE` when the two coincide; a knee that
shifts when the range is shortened by one candidate constitutes weak evidence.
`note` explains every row for which no complete result is available:

| `note` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| empty | a knee was found and is stable |
| `fewer than three candidates` | a line needs three points for a knee |
| `three candidates: stability not assessed` | `stable` needs four points |
| `the criterion does not fall along this line` | no diminishing return to find |
| `the curve does not bend below the line` | the curve is straight or bends upward |
| `no knee when the largest is left out` | the shortened line has no knee |
| `moves when the largest is left out` | the knee depends on the range fitted |

```{r knee-values, include = FALSE}
knees <- get_results(models, "knees")
profile_line <- subset(knees, direction == "profiles" &
                         line == "3 group classes")
knee_three <- with(profile_line, knee_candidate)
knee_three_without <- with(profile_line, knee_without_largest)
knee_three_distance <- with(profile_line, round(distance, 2))
knee_three_stable <- with(profile_line, stable)
```

With three group classes, the knee along the number of profiles is
`r knee_three`, at a distance of `r knee_three_distance`. Without the largest
candidate it is `r knee_three_without`, so `stable` is `r knee_three_stable`:
the bend lies between three and four profiles, and which of the two is
identified depends on the extent of the grid. The deltas locate the same
region with less ambiguity, which is why the two are interpreted jointly.

### The criterion over the whole grid

The heatmap displays all candidates simultaneously, shaded by the difference
between each candidate's criterion and the minimum in the grid. It uses the
same criterion as the deltas and accepts the same `using` argument.

```{r heatmap}
plot_selection(models, what = "heatmap")
```

## Are the classes distinct?

A candidate may fit the data well yet separate its classes poorly, leaving
many units with uncertain class membership. Three statistics derived from the
posterior probabilities of membership quantify separation.

- **Relative entropy**, `1 - EN / (n log K)` for `K` classes, ranges from 0,
  when every unit is equally likely to belong to every class, to 1, when
  every unit is classified with certainty. It summarizes an entire level in a
  single value and is undefined (`NA`) for a level with one class.
- **Average posterior probability (AvePP)** of a class is the mean posterior
  probability of that class among the units modally assigned to it. Values of
  0.7 to 0.8 or above are conventionally taken to indicate adequate
  separation (Nagin, 2005). Being class-specific, it reveals a single poorly
  separated class that entropy would average away.
- **Odds of correct classification (OCC)** of a class is
  `(p / (1 - p)) / (r / (1 - r))`, where `p` is its AvePP and `r` its
  estimated proportion. It compares model-based classification with
  assignment by class proportion alone: values near 1 indicate no
  improvement, and values of 5 or more are conventionally taken to indicate
  adequate separation (Nagin, 2005).

The table of candidates summarizes each level by its relative entropy and the
minimum, maximum and mean AvePP, and counts the classes below a cutoff (0.8 by
default, set with `cutoff`). `get_results(x, "classification")` reports, for
every class of every candidate, its size by modal assignment and by estimate,
its AvePP, its OCC and the relative entropy of its level.

```{r classification}
get_results(models, "classification")
```

`plot_selection(x, what = "diagnostics")` displays relative entropy and the minimum
AvePP across candidates, with the cutoff indicated; `what = "entropy"` and
`what = "avepp"` display either one. For a single fitted candidate,
`plot_diagnostics()` displays the posterior probability of each unit's
assigned class, each unit's relative entropy, the class sizes and the matrix
of average posterior probabilities, for the profiles and, when there are two
or more group classes, for the group classes (`what = "group_posteriors"`,
etc.).

```{r diagnostics}
plot_selection(models, what = "diagnostics")
```

Entropy and AvePP may diverge, and the divergence is informative. AvePP
depends only on the posterior probability of each unit's assigned class,
whereas entropy depends on the full vector of posterior probabilities. A unit
with posterior probabilities of 0.70, 0.10, 0.10 and 0.10 and a unit with 0.70
and 0.30 contribute equally to AvePP, but the former, whose uncertainty is
distributed across all classes, reduces entropy considerably more. Moreover,
entropy is more sensitive to a minority of highly uncertain units than to a
majority of nearly certain ones. A level comprising mostly well-classified
units and a tail of uncertain ones therefore exhibits moderate AvePP
together with low entropy.

The two levels of a two-level model are classified on the basis of different
amounts of information. A group's class is inferred from all of its
observations jointly, whereas an observation's profile is inferred from its
own responses and the group's inferred class, which also uses the other
observations in that group. Certainty at either level depends on the fitted
separation and available information. For a single candidate, `plot_diagnostics()`
displays both levels:

```{r group-certainty}
plot_diagnostics(get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3"),
                 what = "group_posteriors")
```

When all candidates separate their profiles poorly, such that no number of
classes yields adequate entropy or minimum AvePP, the indicators do not
discriminate well among individual observations. The number of classes is
then determined from the information criteria and substantive
interpretation, and the limited separation is reported as a limitation. In
this situation modal class assignments are an unreliable substitute for the
latent classes in subsequent analyses, and bias-corrected three-step
estimators (`r3step()`, `three_step()`) should be used instead.

Classification quality is not in itself a criterion for the number of
classes: models with fewer classes are generally better separated, so
selection on entropy alone favours too few classes. It serves to discriminate
between candidates that the information criteria do not distinguish, and it
determines how the selected classes may be used, for example whether modal
assignments can represent them in subsequent analyses.

## Can the estimate be trusted?

### Estimation checks

Because the likelihood is multimodal, a solution replicated from several random
starts is more credible than one obtained from a single start. An estimate on
the boundary of the parameter space, such as a variance at its lower bound or
a class with negligible membership, indicates a model too complex for the
data. `plot_selection(x, what = "trust")` represents each candidate by a tile labelled
with the number of starts that reached its maximum likelihood and shaded by
the first problem detected:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| best replicated | converged within the interior of the parameter space, with the maximum likelihood reached by more than one start |
| best found once | as above, but the maximum likelihood was reached by a single start |
| on a boundary | an estimate lies on the boundary of the parameter space |
| not converged | the EM algorithm terminated before meeting its convergence criterion |
| not fitted (`x`) | not identified, or estimation failed (the error is retained in the table) |

```{r trust}
plot_selection(models, what = "trust")
```

A candidate whose maximum was found only once should be re-estimated with
more starts before it is selected, together with the remainder of the grid
(see *Random starts*). If re-estimation increases its likelihood, the earlier
solution was a local maximum and is superseded; entropy and AvePP often
increase as well. A higher AvePP is never a ground for preferring one
solution of a given candidate over another: the maximum likelihood solution
is the estimate. The columns `converged`, `boundary`, `n_best_replicated`,
`warnings` and `error` of the table of candidates report the same
diagnostics. A candidate on a boundary whose smallest class holds about one
observation is a degenerate solution rather than a class; re-estimating the
grid with `boundary = "exclude"` replaces it with the best solution in the
interior of the parameter space (see *Random starts*).

### The smallest class

A class comprising a very small proportion of units is difficult to interpret
and is estimated from little data. `plot_selection(x, what = "smallest")` displays the
estimated proportion of the smallest class of every candidate, with a
reference line at 5%, a conventional threshold rather than a rule.

```{r smallest}
plot_selection(models, what = "smallest")
```

## All of the plots together

`plot_selection(x)` returns the deltas, the heatmap, the smallest
class, the estimation diagnostics and the classification diagnostics as a
list of plots displayed in sequence. `using` sets the criterion for the first
two and `cutoff` the AvePP threshold for the last.

```{r selection, fig.height = 5}
plot_selection(models)
```

## How the profiles divide

The clustering tree shows how the profiles of each model are partitioned in the
model with one additional profile: each profile is linked to the profiles of
the larger model that receive its observations (Zappia and Oshlack, 2018). A
profile that divides cleanly into two suggests a substantive distinction,
whereas a profile formed from several profiles of the smaller model suggests
a reallocation of observations rather than a refinement. Each number of
group classes has its own tree, selected with `n_group_classes`; the guide
*Tree plot* compares solutions at one number of profiles.

```{r tree, fig.height = 6}
plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = 1)
```

## Comparing chosen candidates

Once the evidence has reduced the choice to a few candidates,
`compare_models()` tabulates them side by side, specified by label or by
numbers of classes. The table adds each candidate's difference in BIC from the
smallest value among those compared (`delta_bic`) and its BIC weight,
`exp(-delta_bic / 2)` normalized over the compared candidates, which
approximates the posterior probability of each model under equal prior
probabilities, assuming one of them is correct (Wagenmakers and Farrell,
2004). The weights are conditional on the set of candidates compared.

```{r compare}
comparison <- compare_models(models, "profiles3_groups3", "profiles4_groups3",
                             "profiles4_groups2")
comparison
plot(comparison)
```

The fitted model corresponding to a row is extracted with `get_candidate()`,
by label or by numbers of classes.

```{r chosen}
chosen <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
chosen
```

## Testing one more class

The conventional likelihood ratio test is invalid for comparing mixtures with
`k` and `k + 1` classes, because the null model lies on the boundary of the
parameter space of the alternative, where the test statistic does not follow
its usual asymptotic distribution. `bootstrap_lrt()` approximates the null
distribution by parametric bootstrap (McLachlan, 1987; Nylund, Asparouhov and
Muthén, 2007): data sets are simulated from the fitted null model, both
models are re-estimated on each, and the observed statistic is referred to
the simulated distribution. With `B` simulated data sets of which `b` yield a
statistic at least as large as the observed one, the p-value is
`(b + 1) / (B + 1)`, which is bounded below by `1 / (B + 1)`. If any replicate
fails an estimation check, the p-value is withheld rather than computed from
the remaining replicates. The example uses 19 replicates, for which the
smallest attainable p-value is 0.05; applied analyses should use 99 or more.

```{r blrt}
smaller <- get_candidate(models, "profiles3_groups3")
larger <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
test <- bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = course_engagement,
                      iter = 19, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
test
plot(test)
```

The Vuong-Lo-Mendell-Rubin test refers the same statistic to an asymptotic
approximation of its distribution (Vuong, 1989; Lo, Mendell and Rubin, 2001):
a weighted sum of chi-square variables with one degree of freedom, whose
weights are the eigenvalues of a matrix formed from the scores and second
derivatives of both models. The test requires no simulation. Its adjusted
version (aLMR) divides the statistic by `1 + 1 / (d log n)`, with `d` the
number of added parameters and `n` the number of independent units, and
refers it to the same distribution. `get_results()` with `"lmr"` reports both
for every pair of converged candidates that differ by one profile or one group
class. A pair whose information matrix is singular, here the candidates with
five and six profiles, is kept with its reason in `note`.

```{r lmr}
subset(get_results(models, "lmr"), n_group_classes == 3)
```

The regularity conditions of Vuong's theorem do not hold for mixture models
(Jeffries, 2003), and the test's p-values are not uniformly distributed when
the smaller model is true (Vermunt, 2024). It is one piece of evidence beside
the criteria, the classification and the bootstrap.

## Putting the evidence together

No algorithm converts this evidence into a number of classes, and latents
applies none. A defensible decision is reached by examining the evidence in a
fixed sequence and reporting each step:

0. **Analytic decisions**: report the number of random starts, whether
   starts at a variance bound were excluded (`boundary`), any centring or
   scaling, the treatment of missing values, and the number of observations
   with no observed indicator.
1. **Sample-size convention**: specify the convention before examining any
   criterion and apply it consistently.
2. **Criterion minima**: examine the minima under that convention, noting
   where the criteria agree and the direction in which they disagree. A
   minimum at the boundary of the grid requires an extended grid.
3. **Deltas and knees**: where the criteria decrease throughout, examine the
   magnitude of successive decreases and report the knee with its `distance`
   and stability.
4. **Classification quality**: for the remaining candidates, report relative
   entropy and the minimum AvePP and OCC at each level.
5. **Estimation diagnostics**: verify replication of the maximum likelihood,
   the absence of boundary estimates and the size of the smallest class;
   re-estimate candidates whose maximum was found only once.
6. **Likelihood ratio test**: when the evidence is equivocal, test the leading
   candidate against its neighbour with the bootstrap likelihood ratio test.
7. **Substantive interpretation**: among candidates that the statistics do
   not distinguish, select the one whose classes are distinct and
   substantively meaningful for the research question, and state the
   rationale.

The tables underlying each step are returned by the functions above, so that
the reported decision can be reproduced from the reported evidence.

```{r reference, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Call = c(
    "enumerate_classes(..., n_starts = , centering = , scaling = , missing = \"fiml\")",
    "enumerate_classes(..., boundary = \"exclude\")",
    "as.data.frame(models)",
    "get_results(models, \"best\")",
    "plot_enumeration(models), plot_enumeration(models, what = \"bic_groups\"), what = \"all\"",
    "get_results(models, \"deltas\", using = )",
    "plot_selection(models, what = \"deltas\", using = )",
    "get_results(models, \"knees\", using = )",
    "plot_selection(models, what = \"heatmap\", using = )",
    "get_results(models, \"classification\")",
    "get_results(models, \"candidates\", cutoff = )",
    "plot_enumeration(models, what = \"diagnostics\", \"entropy\" or \"avepp\", cutoff = )",
    "get_results(fit, \"entropy\")",
    "plot_diagnostics(fit), what = \"group_posteriors\" and the like",
    "plot_selection(models, what = \"trust\")",
    "plot_selection(models, what = \"smallest\")",
    "plot_selection(models)",
    "plot_tree(models)",
    "compare_models(models, \"name\", ...)",
    "get_candidate(models, \"name\")",
    "bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data, iter)",
    "get_results(models, \"lmr\")"),
  Result = c(
    "The same starts, centring, scaling and missing-data handling for every candidate",
    "Starts with a variance at its lower bound set aside for every candidate",
    "One row per candidate: every criterion, classification summaries and checks",
    "The candidate at the minimum of each criterion and convention",
    "Criteria across the candidates, lowest ringed",
    "Decrease in a criterion from one profile fewer and one group class fewer",
    "The decreases along profiles and along group classes",
    "Chord-distance knee of each line, with its stability",
    "Distance of every candidate from the lowest criterion",
    "Size, AvePP, OCC and entropy of every class of every candidate",
    "The table of candidates with another AvePP cutoff",
    "Relative entropy and lowest AvePP across the candidates",
    "Relative entropy of one fit at each level, over the classified units",
    "Certainty, uncertainty, sizes and AvePP of one fit, profiles and group classes",
    "Convergence, boundary and replication of every candidate",
    "Share of the smallest class of every candidate",
    "Deltas, heatmap, smallest class, trust and diagnostics together",

```
